strengths: MSAM offers a simple, practically useful way to obtain sharpness-aware training benefits with one forward/backward pass, reusing the existing momentum buffer. Its relationship to Nesterov and extragradient methods is clearly explained.

The empirical improvements over baseline optimizers are substantial in several settings. On CIFAR100, WRN-16-4 improves from 76.90% to 79.11%, while the reported aggregate training speed remains approximately that of the baseline. Equal-compute comparisons further support the method’s practical promise.

The extensive ablations on perturbation sign, normalization, learning-rate coupling, alternative directions, and curvature provide useful empirical insights. Compatibility with adaptive and batch-normalization-only perturbations strengthens the contribution.

Training configurations, full hyperparameter sweeps, and a linked code repository support reproducibility. The discussion of instability and computational limitations is informative. No material ethical concern is apparent from the described research.
weaknesses: The generalization guarantee in Appendix A.1 is not established. Proposition 1 is false for negative Hessian trace: with H = diag(-2,-1), standard Gaussian perturbations, and rho = 1, its inequality becomes approximately -0.271 <= -1.5. This Hessian is compatible with Setting 1. Theorem 3 also does not state the population-loss smoothing and loss assumptions needed for the invoked PAC-Bayes argument, or control the Taylor remainder. Consequently, Section 4.1’s claim that improved generalization directly follows from the theory is unsupported.

The principal ViT comparisons use unequal warm-up policies: perturbations are disabled during warm-up for MSAM but retained for SAM. Table A.2 shows that applying the same policy to SAM increases its accuracy to 69.8%, versus MSAM’s 69.1%, weakening the apparent parity in the main results. The disclosure is welcome, but equally tuned schedules are necessary for the comparison.

The model-selection and uncertainty protocols leave important questions unresolved. Appendix A.15 reports the best perturbation strength alongside test-accuracy sweeps without identifying a separate validation-selection procedure. Most ImageNet results use single runs; uncertainty estimated from smaller baseline models cannot establish variability for SAM/MSAM, particularly given the reported instabilities.

Claims of broadly comparable SAM accuracy exceed the demonstrated evidence. MSAM trails SAM by 2.4 percentage points on ViT-S/16 at 300 epochs and 2.0 points on ViT-B/16 at 90 epochs. Equal-compute evaluation on these larger configurations is missing. The results support a promising efficiency–accuracy tradeoff, but do not establish the broad performance claims.

Several mechanistic interpretations remain inconclusive. Projecting MSAM gradients into the SAM/SGD plane can conceal a large orthogonal component, so projected alignment does not establish full-gradient similarity. Likewise, flatter random loss slices do not establish better approximation of the full-dataset sharpness objective. These observations should be distinguished more carefully from explanations of the generalization gains.
